name: hyphy
why: Phylogenetic hypothesis testing software that lets you run real evolutionary analyses on sequence trees at home.

brief.what_it_is: HyPhy (Hypothesis Testing using Phylogenies) is an open-source package for comparative sequence analysis, built on stochastic evolutionary models. It takes a sequence alignment plus a phylogenetic tree (FASTA, NEXUS, Phylip or MEGA input, per the 2.5 README) and runs statistical tests that detect natural selection, recombination, co-evolution and rate variation across genes and lineages. Output is machine-readable JSON, which the companion HyPhy Vision site renders as interactive trees and site plots. It ships as a command-line tool (hyphy), a scripting language called HBL, and a shared library callable from Python and R.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it as a suite of advanced phylogenetic methods for detecting and testing natural selection, recombination, co-evolution and rate variation. The 2.5 README frames it as software for analysing genetic sequences with techniques from phylogenetics, molecular evolution and machine learning, and notes that it powers the datamonkey.org web server.
brief.how_it_works: Each analysis is a named method (for example MEME, FUBAR, FEL, BUSTED, aBSREL, RELAX, GARD) that fits a codon or nucleotide substitution model to an alignment and tree and then tests hypotheses about selection or recombination. Results are written as JSON, which HyPhy Vision parses for visualisation. The homepage lists the analyses as: MEME for episodic site-specific positive selection, FUBAR/FEL/SLAC for pervasive selection, BUSTED/aBSREL for gene-wide and branch-specific selection, RELAX for relaxed or intensified constraint, and GARD for recombination breakpoints.

brief.install_notes: Not available for Windows. Conda or Homebrew are the easy routes; the installation page says you may need to add the bioconda channel first. Building from source needs cmake 3.12 or newer, a C++14-capable compiler (gcc 4.9 or newer per the README), libcurl and pthreads. On macOS, OpenMP comes from brew install libomp. An MPI build needs an MPI library such as OpenMPI on your PATH. The build auto-detects host CPU features (AVX, AVX2); use -DNOAVX=ON for heterogeneous clusters. The HyPhy library path can be set with the LIBPATH argument or the HYPHY_LIB_PATH environment variable. Docker and a WebAssembly build are also described. There are no accounts needed for local use. The installation page says 'please register and download HyPhy' before building from source, but it does not say what registration involves, so treat that as unverified.
brief.standout: You can run the core analyses without installing anything: Datamonkey runs them on a public cluster, and v3.datamonkey.org runs them entirely client-side in the browser, with results viewable in HyPhy Vision. The CLI also accepts every interactive prompt as a positional argument, so even older analyses without flags can be scripted.
brief.status: Maintained, with a mid-transition. The README carries a notice that HyPhy 2.5.x (this repo's legacy line) is in pure maintenance mode with only critical bug fixes, and that active development has moved to HyPhy 3 at github.com/veg/hyphy-3. The homepage lists 2026 publications and tools, so the project is active. I did not see a last-release date or last-commit date, so the exact recency of commits is unknown.
brief.caveats: No Windows support. The legacy 2.5 line is maintenance-only, so new models and methods are in HyPhy 3, which I only skimmed (its README covers C++20, Python and PyTorch bindings, and new methods such as BUSTED-S and dFEL). The homepage and README disagree slightly on the --tree flag in the scripted example. Not every analysis has CLI flags (the README cites acd as an example). Building from source has real dependencies, and OpenMP is missing from some default macOS toolchains. The license page was not fetched, so the licence is unverified. I did not check whether the Homebrew formula tracks 2.5 or 3.
